name: Can I take this book home please?

content.title: Can I take this book home please?
content.summary: Find out how the Biloongra picture book spurred curiousity about road safety in children.

media.alt: Can I take this book home please?

content.text: "Can we take this book home please?" is one of the many questions that research assistant Haris Ahmad was asked during a Grade 4 class in Karachi.
It was a heartfelt plea that Haris and his colleagues were to hear over and over again as they tested how storytelling using an illustrated children's book,
*, about children playing outside could be used to stimulate a discussion on road safety.

"Your football rolls onto the road, what do you do? Should you go and get it?" asks Haris. The students pause and then there's a quick show of hands and a flurry of ideas about how to cross the road. Haris then puts down the book and shows the class a poster about how traffic lights and zebra crossings can help one cross the road safely.
Researchers from the department of emergency medicine at AKU visited 17 schools in Karachi over a four-month period to assess whether children's literature such as the
series could be used to impart key child health messages.

"We wanted to test whether storybooks could help us engage students and draw their attention to potential safety hazards outside the home," said Dr Asad Mian, one of the authors of Biloongra, a faculty member at Aga Khan University, and the principal investigator of the study, said. "It was great to see children identify with the characters and to see them recall the safety tips when we revisited their school two months later."
The researchers were also pleasantly surprised to hear that children went on to share what they learned with their parents and friends.

"Although our study was not set up to gauge the spillover effect on children's peer groups and their parents, literature from elsewhere suggests that such approaches to child health literacy also benefits those not directly related to the study" said Dr Mian. "We're now hoping to use this subtle storytelling approach in our future collaborations to tackle other child health issues such as immunization, hygiene and environmental protection".

The researchers are also considering other initiatives such as adapting the stories so that they can be read on cellphones and tablets, and the creation of translated versions of the book in Hindi for India and Swahili for Africa. The research team is also interested in partnering with AKU's Examination Board and Institute for Educational Development to take the concept further.
The project, whose findings have been published in
, was made possible by a grant through the Johns Hopkins-Pakistan Fogarty International Collaborative Trauma and Injury Training Program.
Uzma Rahim Khan, Nukhba Zia, Rubaba Naeem, Asher Feroze, Amarah Shakoor and Muniba Shah were a part of the team involved in the project.

The Biloongra series of bilingual (Urdu-English) storybooks was developed in Houston, Texas, several years back under the guidance of Bookgroup, an educational and research-oriented children's publishing house in Karachi, Pakistan. Biloongra means kitten in Urdu, but is more commonly used as a term of endearment for a child. All stories in the series revolve around a family of two siblings, their parents and their pet kitten.
